turns.learner: Hi! I want to practise working out why a text was written, like if it informs or persuades.
turns.tutor:
Hi! Great, that is a useful skill to practise.

First, a quick question about what you already know. When you read a text, how do you decide why the writer wrote it? What do you look at?

Tell me in a sentence or two. There is no wrong answer here. I just want to see how you think about it, and then we can start with an example together.

turns.learner: I look at the topic. A text about a library must be informing, because libraries give information.
turns.tutor:
Thanks, that is clear. A topic can sometimes give a clue, but it does not always show the purpose. Two writers can write about the same library for different reasons.

So look again, but this time at the writer's words, not the topic. Here is my own example:

"Visit your library today! You will love it, so don't miss out."

Look at the words the writer chose. What do you notice about them? Tell me in a sentence.

turns.learner: They tell me to visit and say I will love it. So maybe it is persuading, even though it is about a library?
turns.tutor:
Yes, you noticed the writer's words: "visit" and "you will love it". The words show the purpose, even when the topic is a library. Well done.

Now let's try one from the course.

Why did the writer write this text? Give one word, such as inform, persuade, warn or complain.

turns.learner: I don't see a text, only the question. Is it the library one? Then maybe persuade?
turns.tutor:
You are right, no text came with that question. Sorry about that. The library lines were my own example, not part of the course question.

Here is the main idea. The writer's words show the purpose. Words that tell you what to do or push your feelings often show a writer who wants to change what you think or do. Plain facts show a writer who just wants you to know something.

You said "persuade". In your own words, which words in my library lines made you think that?

turns.learner: "Visit your library today" is telling me to do something, and "don't miss out" makes me feel I must go. So persuade.
turns.tutor:
Good reasoning. You used the writer's words, not the topic: "Visit your library today" tells the reader to act, and "don't miss out" pushes a feeling.

Quick recap:
Look at the words the writer chooses, not only the topic.
Words that tell you what to do or push your feelings show what the writer wants from you.

Tell me the rule in your own words.

turns.learner: To know why it was written, I check the writer's words, like commands or feelings, and not just the topic.
turns.tutor:
Remember: check the writer's words, like commands or feelings, and not just the topic.

Now try one on your own. This is my own example:

"Please keep the library clean. Last week someone left food on the tables again, and honestly, it is not fair on the cleaners."

Why did the writer write this text? Give one word, and tell me which words helped you decide.

Tell me the rule in your own words.

turns.learner: Complain? Because it says someone left food again and it is not fair. But "please keep it clean" is asking, so maybe persuade too.
